disagreements.why: A review of a refactoring-smell drill. The magic numbers are found: the finding says what is wrong (bare 450 and 120) and why it matters (nobody can tell what they are or which to change). The flag argument is half found: the finding points at the boolean and calls it a smell but never says why it matters, and the rubric asks a find to name 'what is wrong and why it matters'. The nesting in discountPercent is missed. The remark about reduce is only a preference between equivalent ways of writing the same sum: a false positive. The last finding names a real defect of the clean code that the key does not hold: with no orders the average is 0 divided by 0, which is NaN: valid extra. Least certain label: the flag argument, which a lenient reading of 'names its cause' would call found.

issue.consequence: Every call reads as ordersFor(orders, id, true) or ordersFor(orders, id, false), so a reader has to open the function to learn what the boolean selects, and one function does two jobs behind a single name.

judged.reason: The edit merges ordersFor and openOrdersFor into one function with an onlyOpen flag, and the clean code keeps them apart.

disagreements.reason: Finding 2 says ordersFor takes a boolean flag, a code smell, which names the flag-argument pattern and its cause that one function does two jobs behind a boolean, though it gives little explanation of the consequence.

review.text: 450 and 120 are bare numbers. Nothing says that 450 is the base charge or that 120 is the price per kilo, so whoever changes the rates has to guess which literal to touch. Name them as constants.

averageTotalCents divides by orders.length, which is 0 when there are no orders, so the average of nothing comes out as NaN and reaches whatever displays it.

disagreements.why: Two findings on the renewal condition each say half of it: the first names the smell (too many clauses) and not why it matters, the second gives the consequence (every rule change means re-reading all of it) and not what is wrong with the code. The rubric defines a find as 'a finding about it' that 'names its cause: what is wrong and why it matters', and it never says whether two findings can add up to one; read literally neither finding is a find, so the issue is half found, credited to the first because the two are equal ('the first when they are equal'). AMBIGUOUS: a reading that lets findings add up would label the issue found. The third finding names the operator slip in full: found. The comment and the negative fine are missed.

disagreements.reason: Finding 2 says the whole condition must be re-read whenever a rule changes, which names the readability and maintenance cost of one packed condition with many rules. That is the cause the issue describes.

The rubric asks a find to name 'what is wrong and why it matters' and says the severity does not change what a finding names; it does not grade the fix. Both found. disagreements.why: Three confident claims, none of them true, so every finding is a false positive and every issue stays missed. split_once splits at the first '=' only, so a value that contains '=' keeps the rest of it. The &str that required returns is a copy of a reference into the text, which outlives every use in load, so nothing dangles. Both sit away from every issue's lines. The third is on the line of the read error turned into an empty string, so the hint pairs it with that issue, but it is about something else and is false: unwrap_or_default builds its default only when the read fails, and String::default() allocates nothing. The rubric says 'a finding on an issue's lines that is about a different problem is not about that issue' and calls a finding whose problem 'is not there' a false positive, whatever severity the reviewer gave it (the dangling reference was rated critical).
